messages.subject: posterior samples - negative binomial model
parts:
Dear all,

I am working on modeling the effects of climate and landscape on mosquito abundance. Right now, I am working on a model to explore how the wind speed affects the trap effectiveness, with the idea of incorporating this effect into the final model.

I am using jagsUI, and mostly following examples in the AHM books and adapting them to my case study. However, I have little expertise in Bayesian statistics and I am finding some problems in carrying on model checking.

My most basic model right now looks like this:

model{
#likelihood
for (i in 1:N){
  captures[i] ~ dnegbin(p[i], r)
  p[i] <- r/(r+lambda[i])
  log(lambda[i]) <-  alpha[week_num[i]] + beta1*wind2[i]
 
}
#random effect
for(j in 1:M){
  alpha[j] ~ dnorm(mu.alpha, tau.alpha) # Mean and precision = 1/variance
}

#priors
beta1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
mu.alpha~dnorm(0, 0.001)
tau.alpha ~ dgamma(1.0E-3, 1.0E-3)
sigma.alpha <- sqrt(1/tau.alpha)
r ~ dunif(0,50)
}

Some colleagues recommended sampling from the posterior distribution of the model’s parameter and developing simulated data to visually compare is they are similar to the observed data or not, as a part of model checking and fit assessment. For this, I thought of doing something similar to AHM Book1 5.9:

# Likelihood of the model
for (i in 1:M){
Cmax[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i]) # note no variance parameter
log(lambda[i]) <- alpha[facFor[i]] + beta[facFor[i]] * elev[i]
resi[i] <- (Cmax[i]-lambda[i]) / (sqrt(lambda[i])+e) # Pearson residual
}

#simulated data
lambda2 <- array(dim = c(15000, 267))
for(j in 1:267){ # Loop over sites
lambda2[,j] <- exp(out5$sims.list$alpha[,facFor[j]] +
out5$sims.list$beta[,facFor[j]] * elev[j]) # linear regression/backtransform
}

However, I do not understand if this would be correct for a negative binomial distribution.

I also noticed that for some fit assessment approaches it is necessary to add a simulated data set like captures.new[i] ~ dnegbin(p[I], r) on the model itself. In this case, are we doing the same as in the previous example? 

I also thought about using a test statistic to complement the GoF assessment, but I am not sure how I should choose between different options. For example, I have found mixed opinions on whether the Chi-square test statistic would be appropriate or not for a negative binomial distribution.

My apologies if this post results are too beginner-level for this group, but I have been struggling for some time with the model assessment. I would appreciate it if anyone could give me some advice regarding this issue or recommend any bibliography, website or post on the subject.

Cheers,
Sonia.

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: AW: posterior samples - negative binomial model
parts:
Dear Sonia

 

What your colleagues suggested is called a posterior predictive check for goodness of fit (see Gelman et al. 1996 and Conn et al., Ecol. Mono, 2018). It’s based on the following sensible idea: if a model fits your data, then when you simulate new data under that model (using the values of parameters as estimated from your data), then these data should resemble your actual data.

 

So you have to add in your code one or more lines that produce samples from the predictive distribution of the data. The simplest way to do this would be to add the red bit in your first block of code below. When you monitor captures.new, you will get one sampled value of each datum i at every iteration of the MCMC algorithm.

 

Note that there is a twist here for hierarchical models like yours, where you may simulate new data either based on the estimated random effects or else you may also resample new values for the random effects (the alpha’s in your case). I don’t go into this but refer you to the vignette “DHARMa for Bayesians” in the R package DHARMa (Hartig, see below).

 

There are multiple ways in which you can make a comparison between the actual data and the data that would be expected under the model under the assumption that the model fits your actual data (i.e., captures.new). One is to calculate some omnibus test statistic such as chisquared or Freeman-Tukey, which are based on the expected values of your response and thus are a function of model residuals.

 

One pretty widely used R package for goodness of fit assessment in traditional mixed models is DHARMa. There is a vignette that explains how you can use it with existing Bayesian simulations produced by software such as JAGS. Perhaps I’d simply suggest to you to use that.

 

Best regards  --- Marc
